master_output.idea:
**Mocking:** World-class AI researcher

Let me start from what the training script is doing, not from a recipe. The code runs a fixed number of epochs with a fixed learning rate and batch size. That's a decision, not a law. The decision rule I want to interrogate: why accept a single fixed hyperparameter setting when the objective landscape is almost surely non-convex and the optimal setting is likely not uniform across the data? I'm a researcher, so I'll treat this as a hypothesis to be falsified, not a fact to be obeyed.

Here's the move I keep coming back to: search the hyperparameter space instead of guessing. Grid search is the default, but it's a brute-force trap — it samples regularly, so it can miss sharp valleys and it wastes compute on regions that don't matter. The smarter choice is a Bayesian optimizer. Why Bayesian? Because it builds a probabilistic model of the objective and chooses the next point to probe by maximizing expected improvement — it actively learns where to look, not just covers ground. This is the mechanism that makes it non-trivial and worth spending on a few epochs rather than the whole budget.

Now, the honest constraint: I'm allowed only 10 epochs. That means I can't afford to run many full training runs. So I have to make each run count. That's where transfer learning cuts in — I don't start from random weights, I start from a pretrained model. The pretrained weights act as an informative prior over the parameters, so the search can jump toward good regions faster. This is the free lunch that lets a short search still yield strong results: a small number of runs on a pretrained model is effectively a large number on random weights.

How I keep myself honest: I don't declare victory until the optimizer has found a good setting and the validation metric stops improving. If early stopping shows the metric is still rising, I keep the search going — the search is only as good as its patience. And I validate against the baseline with the same epoch budget, because a faster optimizer only pays off if it beats the same compute, not if it's slower and prettier.

**Core idea:** Replace fixed hyperparameters with a Bayesian optimizer over a pretrained model to search for the best setting in the small budget of 10 epochs.

**Non-trivial crux:** The Bayesian optimizer gains its value from a good prior (pretrained weights) and from early stopping — without both, the short search can't reliably find a good setting.
